parts.note: knocked-down reads as reduced in price, and an adding machine is something that counts, so a shop's counter of marked-down goods

explanation.surface: A calculator that has been toppled over, or sold off cheaply at auction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked-down' suggests something toppled or sold at auction; here it means sold at a reduced price, and the 'adding machine' is a counter, something that counts.
explanation.definitionFit: A shop table of reduced-price goods is a place where discounted items are displayed, and a counter is also a device that counts.

indicators.note: a still is a distilling apparatus that works its contents over, so the letters of the preceding words are reworked

explanation.surface: Someone who has grown fatter remains happy about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'content' looks like an adjective meaning happy, but it is a noun: the fat content of milk. 'still' signals rearranging FATTER and BUT.
explanation.definitionFit: The fat in milk, measured as a proportion of the milk, is its fat content.

clue.text: Concerning the plot, it has its draw back.

parts.note: re means concerning, as in a letter heading
a tract is a plot or stretch of land

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a scheme or piece of land has a drawback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'draw back' reads as the noun drawback, but it is the verb meaning to withdraw or pull back.
explanation.definitionFit: To withdraw something said, or pull something in, is a synonym of drawing it back.

clue.text: Pertaining to a cultural study or a coming change.

indicators.note: change tells the solver to alter the order of the letters in the words before it

explanation.surface: Something relates to cultural studies or to an approaching change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cultural' hides agri-culture: the study is of crop growing, not culture in the arts sense. 'change' signals rearranging OR A COMING.
explanation.definitionFit: Agronomy is the science of soil and crop production, the study of agriculture, and the adjective relates to it.

clue.text: Simply not done-not as a homonym of a synonym.

definitions.text: not as a homonym of a synonym

indicators.note: the word done is simply not to be read as written, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something just is not done, a riddle about words that sound alike and words that mean alike.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a riddle: 'not' sounds like knot, and a synonym of knot is the answer. 'Simply not' tells you to rearrange DONE.
explanation.definitionFit: A knot in a stem or rope is a lump or joint, also called a node, and knot sounds like the word not.

parts.note: the word roods can be formed by rearranging the letters taken from the word doors, so the instruction describes the answer

explanation.surface: A question about how roods, old units of land, might be produced.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as an instruction: OUT OF signals an anagram, and DOORS rearranged gives ROODS. A rood is an old measure of land, a quarter of an acre.
explanation.definitionFit: Being outside rather than in a building is being in the open air.

clue.text: (hyphenated) Mrs. White of the early cinema days?

definitions.text: Mrs. White of the early cinema days?

parts.words: Mrs. White of the early cinema days
parts.note: Pearl White was a star of silent film serials, so her mother would be the mother of Pearl, the shiny lining of shells

explanation.surface: A question about the wife of a Mr White who acted in silent films.
explanation.walkthrough: Pearl White starred in early film serials such as The Perils of Pauline. 'Mrs. White' read as her mother gives mother-of-pearl.
explanation.definitionFit: Mother-of-pearl is the iridescent lining of oyster shells, and Pearl White's mother is cryptically a mother of Pearl.

clue.text: Sir, if you call me that, you do!

definitions.text: Sir, if you call me that, you do!

parts.words: Sir, if you call me that, you do
parts.note: addressing someone with an honorific such as Sir confers a title on them, which is what the verb means

explanation.surface: Someone tells another person that calling them Sir has a certain effect.
explanation.definitionFit: To give someone a title or a right is to confer a name or honour on them.

indicators.note: now, in the present day, the actress's name appears with its first letter moved to the end

parts.note: Eleonora Duse was a celebrated Italian actress who died in 1924

explanation.surface: A one-time Italian actress has found a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'now' signals moving the D of DUSE to the end. 'Former' just places Duse in the past.
explanation.definitionFit: Something put to service has been put to use.

clue.text: Taught to make tea on a bad detour.

parts.note: tea is spelt as the letter T

indicators.note: a bad version of the word detour is one that is muddled into new order

explanation.surface: Someone learns to brew tea while on an unpleasant diversion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to make' and 'on a' are only links; 'bad' is the anagram signal, not a description of the trip.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone instructed privately by a tutor has been taught.

clue.text: The historian stands silent before us.

indicators.note: before places the first piece in front of the second

parts.note: tacit means silent or unspoken

explanation.surface: A historian stays quiet in front of an audience.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacitus was a Roman writer of the Annals and Histories, a historian of imperial Rome.

parts.note: in Arthurian legend and Tennyson's Idylls of the King, the maid of Astolat dies for love of Lancelot

explanation.surface: A title from Arthurian romance.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a plain definition from Tennyson's Idylls of the King: the lily maid of Astolat is a heroine of the Arthurian tales.
explanation.definitionFit: Tennyson's Arthurian heroine, who loves Lancelot and dies, is named and nicknamed so in Malory and the Idylls.

annotationWithheld.why: Deft face, but artificial. — anagram of DEFT FACE with no indicator other than 'artificial', which is also the definition: one word doing two jobs

clue.text: Causes a doctor-bill-when it's paid, hit her for it.

indicators.note: for it says the preceding letters are to be rearranged to give the thing that causes the bill

explanation.surface: An illness runs up a medical bill, and once it is settled someone strikes a woman over it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for it' signals rearranging PAID and HIT HER. The surface's violence is a red herring.
explanation.definitionFit: A serious bacterial infection of the throat is an illness that sends patients to a physician, running up fees.

parts.note: a seaport on the Gulf of Mexico in the state of Tamaulipas

explanation.definitionFit: A Gulf coast city in Tamaulipas is a major Mexican harbour for oil.

clue.text: Water this in the garden, perhaps.

definitions.text: Water this in the garden, perhaps.

parts.words: Water this in the garden, perhaps
parts.note: put water before it for one salad plant, and garden before it for another

explanation.surface: An instruction to water a plant in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Water' looks like a verb, but it is a word to add in front: watercress, and garden cress.
explanation.definitionFit: A peppery salad plant comes as watercress and garden cress, so both words can precede it.

indicators.note: married here means joined and mixed together, so the following letters are blended into a new order

explanation.surface: A man called Peter wed a woman on the French Riviera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'married' signals rearranging HER AT NICE. Peter the Great of Russia married the woman who became Empress, though not at Nice.
explanation.definitionFit: Peter the Great's second wife, later Empress of Russia, bore this name.

clue.text: The top part's as hot as the bottom, with these for protection.

parts.note: the sun is up above and hot, so the top part's is the sun's
Hades, the underworld, is the hot place at the bottom

explanation.surface: Something's upper half is as warm as its lower half, so a cover is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: The sun up top and Hades below are both hot. Here the 's of 'part's' gives an S.
explanation.definitionFit: Parasols and awnings shield people from strong light and heat.

clue.text: Subject to change in a timeless form of 14.

indicators.note: to change means the letters left after the removal are to be rearranged

parts.note: the answer to 14 across, a Mexican port
a time is AM, the morning hours, here taken out by the word less

explanation.surface: Something liable to alteration in a form of a Mexican seaport.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'timeless' has to be split in two: 'a time' is AM (morning), and 'less' takes it away. 14 refers to the answer at 14 across.
explanation.definitionFit: A subject under discussion is the theme or matter being talked about.

parts.note: learners often hit a stage where progress levels off for a while, a flat stretch in the learning curve

explanation.surface: Something students commonly arrive at.
explanation.definitionFit: A stage of stalled progress is like a flat highland: no rise for a while.

parts.note: a professor is one who professes a faith, so one who professes beliefs against church doctrine

explanation.surface: An unconventional university teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'professor' suggests an academic, but here it means one who professes a religion.
explanation.definitionFit: A dissenter from church doctrine professes beliefs that are unorthodox.

annotationWithheld.why: Look! It's in a ruminant! — wordplay LO inside CAMEL, but no clue word defines the purgative compound

parts.note: bucks are dollars, and passing money round to others means distributing riches

explanation.surface: A play on passing the buck, avoiding responsibility.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'pass the buck' means shifting blame; here the plural bucks are dollars handed round.
explanation.definitionFit: Distributing riches among everyone means handing round the money.

clue.text: Stuff oneself with too much eats.

indicators.note: too much of the food leaves it churned up, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone gorges on far too much food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'too much' signals rearranging EATS.
explanation.definitionFit: To fill someone full of food is to satisfy their appetite completely.

parts.note: an era is a period of time

explanation.surface: A question about time dedicated to a goddess of inspiration.
explanation.definitionFit: The Muse of love poetry is one of the nine daughters of Zeus.

indicators.note: flowing means the letters of the word robe are set in motion and rearranged

explanation.surface: A loose, long garment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flowing' signals rearranging ROBE; a river is a flowing thing.
explanation.definitionFit: A river of northern Spain flows to the Mediterranean.

definitions.meaning: full to the top, as a cup filled to the edge
having a projecting edge round the crown, as most hats do

explanation.definitionFit: Full to the top edge, and also having a rim, as a hat does.

clue.text: Get our labor a raise, in the light of spectacular production.

indicators.note: a spectacular production is a showy reworking, so these letters are staged in a new order

explanation.surface: A call for a pay rise for workers, in light of a big show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raise' looks like a pay demand; with OUR LABOR A it is the anagram fodder, rearranged by 'spectacular production'. 'Get' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The northern lights are a natural glowing display in the polar sky.
